title: Why graphs resist sharding
description: Sharding works when a query names its shard. A graph traversal does the opposite: it discovers where to go next only after reading the previous hop.

nodes.label: An edge is a cross-shard fact
nodes.sublabel:
Alice (shard 1) follows Zoe (shard 3).
The relationship belongs to neither
machine, so every traversal is a
scatter-gather waiting to happen.

nodes.label: What actually helps
nodes.sublabel:
• store the adjacency list denormalised
  so one hop is one read
• replicate very-high-degree nodes
• co-locate communities on a shard
• cap traversal depth in the API

steps.text: "Who does Alice follow?" The query names Alice, so it names her shard.
One shard, one read. If the adjacency list is stored denormalised — Alice's followees as a list on her row — this is a single lookup rather than a join, and it is as fast as any other sharded query.
"Who do Alice's followees follow?" Hop one returns a list of user IDs — and those IDs are scattered across every shard, because hashing deliberately destroyed locality.
Hop two must therefore query every shard. Latency is set by the slowest one, and the fan-out grows with each additional hop. Depth 3 on a well-connected graph can touch most of the cluster.

This is the fundamental tension: sharding needs the query to name its shard up front, and a traversal only learns where to go next after reading the previous hop. No shard key fixes that — it is a property of the access pattern.
Denormalise the adjacency list so the common one-hop query never joins. Storage is cheap; cross-shard reads are not.

Replicate very-high-degree nodes — the accounts everyone follows — onto every shard, so traversals through them stay local. The same celebrity asymmetry as the news feed, solved the same way: handle the small expensive set differently.

And cap depth in the API. "Friends of friends" is a product feature; unbounded traversal is a denial-of-service vector against your own database. If deep traversal is genuinely core, that is the argument for a purpose-built graph database rather than a sharded relational one.
